extracted.intended_audience: artists, art historians, and educated readers of Ruskin interested in sculpture, iconography, and architectural ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for interpreting and assessing iconography, symbolism, craftsmanship, and stylistic dating in medieval and early Renaissance sculptural capitals and reliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of iconographic symbols (Hope vs Faith)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols must be accurate to the virtue they signify — e.g., 'anchor is the characteristic not of Hope, but of Faith. Faith is dependent, but Hope is aspirant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer symbols that express the correct theological/conceptual quality of the virtue. Example: Giotto's Hope is winged and aspirant; Spenser's use of an anchor for Hope is called 'inaccurate' and 'vulgarized.' Anti-pattern: adopting conventional but conceptually wrong emblems (anchor for Hope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting Charity as love-animated rather than mere munificence
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar beauty of most of the Italian conceptions of Charity is 'in the subjection of mere munificence to the glowing of her love, always represented by flames.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing Charity, foreground the affective motive (love, often shown as flame or cross-of-fire) over simple acts of giving. Examples: Arena Chapel—circular glory, cross of fire, vase of corn and fruit, receiving treasure from Christ; Dante's 'inflaming her whole form.' Anti-pattern: depicting Charity as mere distribution of goods without emotional/divine signifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active weighing in Justice iconography
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice should be shown as actively weighing causes: 'equality of the scales of Justice is not owing to natural laws, but to her own immediate weighing the opposed causes in her own hands.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compositional choices (e.g., one scale in each hand) to convey that Justice is an active, deliberate power. Examples: Giotto's Justice holds a scale in each hand and juxtaposes an executioner with an angel to show moral weighing. Anti-pattern: passive balance-beam imagery that implies automatic or impersonal balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence must symbolize forethought/anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence's 'truly distinctive character, namely, forethought, is never enough insisted upon' in many representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize anticipatory aspects of Prudence (forethought, vigilance) via attributes such as Janus-headedness, convex mirror (viewing many things), and compasses (measurement). Example: Giotto uses Janus-headed and convex mirror to suggest vigilance and the power to 'look at many things in small compass.' Anti-pattern: reducing Prudence to mere worldly caution without symbolic cues for anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bodily attributes to express moral character
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical features and deformities are used to symbolize inner moral states — e.g., Envy: 'fingers terminating in claws, and raising her right hand with an expression partly of impotent regret, partly of involuntary grasping; a serpent, issuing from her mouth... long membranous ears, horns on her head, and flames consuming her body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design physiognomy and bodily detail to communicate psychological traits (claws for grasping envy, serpents for poisonous speech, large ears for quick hearing). Examples: Giotto's subtle bodily signs vs cruder later renderings. Anti-pattern: neutral or decorative corporeality that fails to embody moral meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate restrained vs violent anger in depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation should distinguish restrained Anger (infinitely more terrible) from violent Rage; 'both of them [Giotto and Spenser] make him violent' and miss the more terrible restrained form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting Wrath, consider depicting the more psychologically potent restrained anger (controlled but terrible) instead of only explosive violence. Anti-pattern: only showing fury and firebrands without subtle signs of controlled, simmering wrath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate similar vices (avarice vs covetousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is curious that most moralists confuse avarice with covetousness, although they are vices totally different in their operation on the human heart, and on the frame of society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about moral distinctions in iconography: avarice as hard love of money (root of certain evils) versus covetousness as inordinate desire for a particular good (different social and moral effects). Choose attributes that reflect these operational differences. Anti-pattern: lumping related sins together and using interchangeable imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey meaning through subtle details and 'few touches'
rubrics_metrics.description: Early sculpture 'appreciat[es] the signs of dignity of character in the features, and the way in which it can exalt the principal figure in any subject by a few touches.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small, deliberate details (a worn portesse, a buckle shaped like a cloven heart, a particular curl of drapery) to convey deep character and narrative. Example: the 'wearing' of the portesse signals abuse of books by idle readers; a few well-chosen touches can elevate the principal figure more than elaborate detail. Anti-pattern: heavy-handed accumulation of ornament without purposeful signification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and intent outrank mere technical virtuosity
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Five hundred men may be now found who could have cut the drapery, as such, far better, for one who would have disposed its folds with this intention.' (on the moon's rippling drapery that suggests moonlight)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value thoughtful arrangement and expressive intent (how folds fall, how drapery ripples) above mere technical polish. Example: Moon's drapery 'ripples down to her feet' to suggest moonlight on waves — superior to technically 'better' carving lacking intent. Anti-pattern: prioritizing virtuoso execution of isolated elements without an expressive plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spatial arrangement to encode astrological/chronological meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of planetary figures and their 'houses' can 'indicate, by the position in which they are placed, the period of the year at which this great corner-stone was laid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the order and orientation of figures (planets, zodiac signs) as potential intentional encodings of time, ritual, or cosmological meaning. Example: the eighteenth capital's arrangement of Sun, Moon, planets interpreted as houses and possibly a date-marker. Anti-pattern: assuming decorative order is arbitrary without testing for encoded meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of color and inlay as expressive elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The inlaying of colored stones 'is merely an expression of the architect's feeling of the essential importance of this art of inlaying, and of the value of color generally in his own art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even small colored inlays or use of polychrome materials should be read as intentional expressive choices by the maker. Do not dismiss minor colored details as mere ornament; they can signal aesthetic priorities. Anti-pattern: treating color as secondary or negligible in architectural sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic details as chronological markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtle stylistic features (e.g., 'the peculiar way in which the ear is cut into the shape of a ring, jagged or furrowed on the edge') are period markers: 'the moment we reach the Renaissance work, the lions' ears are smooth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small formal traits (treatment of ears, drapery, hair, carving edges) to help date works and distinguish schools. Example: jagged ears as fourteenth-century marker; smooth ears for Renaissance. Anti-pattern: relying only on broad motifs or inscriptions for dating when stylistic markers are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some moral qualities are difficult to express visually (e.g., Vanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is difficult to find this sin... definitely expressed in art.' Some vices/virtues resist direct pictorial treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of visual language; some states (subtle vanity, complex inward dispositions) may require allegory, narrative context, or borrowed literary forms to be communicated effectively. Anti-pattern: forcing awkward or literal symbols that fail to capture the moral nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match iconography to historical and cultural context
rubrics_metrics.description: Representations should reflect their era's conception (e.g., medieval Cupid is 'a terrible trinity' allied with Satan and Death, while Renaissance Cupid appears as a beautiful god and plaything of the Graces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select iconographic type appropriate to the cultural-historical viewpoint being expressed: medieval terror vs Renaissance charm will carry very different meanings. Anti-pattern: anachronistic mixing of conceptions that undermines intended moral or historical message.
